text: PhD applicants mostly apply on their own. The hard parts are finding advisors who actually fit, and ten programs with slightly different rules. HiOffer is a careful agent that takes you from school list to offer, and shows its sources.

Six modules, one conversation: find programs, check requirements, assess advisors, assemble materials, support the process, interview and decide. Each is a page you can manage, and things the agent does for you.
Each applicant has a workspace behind an invite code. Inside, HiOffer opens with a brief: three programs, eight verified advisors, nine to-dos due this month, and what to do next.

Ask for the best-fit advisors at UW. The agent calls its tools, then answers with a card: identity anchored by two sources, recent papers verified on OpenAlex, and whether she says she is taking students.

Ask for the drafts: a statement within the limit, a fit paragraph per advisor, an outreach email each. Every sentence is tagged to the applicant's files or a verified paper, and every cited paper is re-checked on OpenAlex. You copy. HiOffer never sends.

The timeline holds what only a human can do, dated from the official deadlines. Programs are also places: climate from Open-Meteo, four rankings, and living notes labelled as general knowledge, on a map.

And a mock interview. A stand-in professor asks what this advisor would plausibly ask, from your materials and their papers; you answer out loud. Each answer gets what worked, what to improve, and the interviewer's impression moves up or down.

Every run is one neatlogs trace: a span per sub-agent and per tool call, with tokens and latency. Run one died on a malformed JSON reply; the trace shows the exact error. In run three the verifier caught the writer inventing a paper, and the trace led to the real bug in my OpenAlex filter.
A neatlogs detection then caught a connector span failing silently inside run five. Fixed the same hour. Pruning old tool results halved input tokens; a full program run now costs eighty-three cents.

Entire recorded every coding session behind every commit: more than fifty checkpoints in two days. Checkpoint explain shows the intent and the files; entire why traces one line back to the conversation that wrote it.

Pricing comes from the traces. In cfo.ai, a forty-nine dollar season pass needs cost under nineteen sixty for a sixty percent margin; we measure eighty-three cents per program. And one surprise: with sales peaking in autumn, a hundred-fifty-thousand-dollar raise runs out of cash before year two's peak.
Nothing invented, nothing missed, nothing sent without you. Everything is public: the repo, the build log, the traces, the plan. HiOffer, built in public for neatHack.
